# Unit 2: Targeting methods, nanoparticles and liposomes — types, preparation and evaluation

Unit 1 explained *why* a carrier goes where it goes. This unit is about the two carriers the syllabus names — **nanoparticles** and **liposomes** — and about the **methods** by which any carrier is aimed at a target. Expect the formulation, the method of preparation and the evaluation table to carry most of the marks.

## 2.1 Targeting methods — an organised list

| Method | Principle | Typical example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Passive | Natural fate of the carrier plus pathology of the tissue (MPS uptake, EPR, capillary blockade) | Liposomal amphotericin B to liver and spleen; PEGylated liposomal doxorubicin to tumours |
| Active, ligand-mediated | Ligand–receptor recognition on the target cell | Folate, transferrin, galactose, mannose, RGD, hyaluronic acid, aptamers |
| Active, antibody-mediated | Antigen–antibody binding | Immunoliposomes, antibody-coated nanoparticles, antibody–drug conjugates |
| Physical / stimulus-responsive | External or local trigger | Magnetic, thermosensitive, pH-sensitive, redox-sensitive, ultrasound- and light-triggered |
| Inverse | Suppress or saturate the MPS first | Pre-dose of blank carrier or dextran sulfate |
| Dual / double / combination | Carrier adds its own effect; or space + time control; or two ligands | Antiviral carrier with antiviral drug; transferrin + cell-penetrating peptide |
| Cell-mediated | Living cells as carriers | Resealed erythrocytes, macrophages, stem cells |
| Prodrug-based | Site-specific activation | ADEPT, GDEPT, colon-targeted azo and polysaccharide prodrugs |

### Ligand coupling chemistry (postgraduate detail)

A ligand can be attached to a carrier in four ways:

1. **Physical adsorption** — simple but reversible and poorly controlled.
2. **Direct covalent coupling to the carrier surface** — carbodiimide (EDC/NHS) chemistry between surface –COOH and ligand –NH2; glutaraldehyde; maleimide–thiol coupling to cysteine residues.
3. **Coupling to the distal end of a PEG chain** (the preferred method) — the ligand stands above the steric layer and remains accessible. Functional PEG derivatives used: maleimide-PEG-DSPE, NHS-PEG-DSPE, and PEG with carboxyl, amine, thiol or azide ends.
4. **Non-covalent affinity coupling** — biotin–avidin/streptavidin bridges; also "click" chemistry (azide–alkyne) and post-insertion of ligand-PEG-lipid micelles into preformed liposomes.

Points to add in an answer: the reaction must not denature the ligand; for an antibody, coupling through the Fc region or through carbohydrate residues keeps the antigen-binding sites free; ligand density matters — too few ligands give weak binding, too many increase immune clearance and can reduce tumour penetration.

## 2.2 Nanoparticles

**Nanoparticles** are solid colloidal carriers of roughly 10–1000 nm (most injectable systems are below about 300 nm) in which the drug is dissolved, entrapped, encapsulated, adsorbed or covalently attached.

### a. Types

| Type | Structure and note |
| --- | --- |
| Nanospheres | Matrix type: drug dispersed throughout the polymer |
| Nanocapsules | Reservoir type: liquid (oily or aqueous) core inside a polymer shell |
| Solid lipid nanoparticles (SLN) | Solid lipid core (glyceryl behenate, stearic acid, tripalmitin) stabilised by surfactant; aqueous dispersion, no organic solvent needed |
| Nanostructured lipid carriers (NLC) | Blend of solid and liquid lipid, giving an imperfect crystal lattice, higher loading and less drug expulsion on storage than SLN |
| Polymeric micelles | Self-assembled core–shell structure from amphiphilic block copolymers (PEG-PLA, PEG-PCL, Pluronics), about 10–100 nm, for poorly soluble drugs |
| Dendrimers | Monodisperse, regularly branched polymers built generation by generation around a core (PAMAM, PPI, polylysine); drug solubilised in internal cavities or conjugated to surface groups; high surface functionality but cationic generations are haemolytic and cytotoxic, which is reduced by PEGylation or surface acetylation |
| Nanocrystals | Pure drug nanocrystals stabilised by surfactant; raise saturation solubility and dissolution rate (Ostwald–Freundlich and Noyes–Whitney) |
| Inorganic | Gold, silica (including mesoporous silica), iron oxide (magnetic, also an MRI contrast agent), quantum dots, carbon nanotubes |
| Protein and polysaccharide based | Albumin, gelatin, chitosan, alginate nanoparticles |

### b. Polymers and excipients

- **Synthetic biodegradable**: poly(lactic acid) (PLA), poly(lactide-co-glycolide) (PLGA — degradation rate set by the lactide:glycolide ratio and molecular weight), polycaprolactone (slow), poly(alkyl cyanoacrylates) (fast, surface erosion), polyanhydrides, polyorthoesters.
- **Natural**: chitosan (cationic, mucoadhesive, permeation enhancing), alginate, gelatin, albumin, dextran, hyaluronic acid.
- **Stabilisers and surfactants**: poloxamers, polysorbates, polyvinyl alcohol, lecithin, sodium cholate, TPGS.
- **Cryoprotectants** for freeze-drying: mannitol, trehalose, sucrose, lactose.

### c. Methods of preparation

**From preformed polymers**

1. **Emulsification–solvent evaporation.** Polymer and drug are dissolved in a volatile water-immiscible solvent (dichloromethane, ethyl acetate), emulsified into an aqueous surfactant solution by high-speed homogenisation or sonication, and the solvent is evaporated under reduced pressure so that the polymer hardens into nanospheres. For water-soluble drugs a **double emulsion (w/o/w)** is used. Size is controlled by stirring/sonication energy, surfactant type and concentration, polymer concentration and phase-volume ratio.
2. **Nanoprecipitation (solvent displacement, Fessi method).** Polymer and drug in a water-miscible solvent (acetone, ethanol) are added dropwise to an aqueous phase containing a stabiliser. Rapid diffusion of the solvent lowers the polymer's solubility and it precipitates as nanoparticles (Marangoni effect). Simple, reproducible, gives small particles; suited to lipophilic drugs.
3. **Emulsification–solvent diffusion.** A partially water-miscible solvent (benzyl alcohol, propylene carbonate) saturated with water is used; dilution with a large volume of water makes the solvent diffuse out and the particles form.
4. **Salting-out.** Acetone solution of polymer is emulsified into an aqueous solution saturated with an electrolyte (magnesium acetate) or sucrose, which prevents mixing; dilution with water then drives acetone out. Avoids chlorinated solvents.
5. **Supercritical fluid methods** (RESS, SAS) — supercritical CO2 as solvent or antisolvent; solvent-free and attractive for heat- and solvent-sensitive drugs.
6. **Spray drying** and **nano spray drying**.

**By polymerisation of monomers**

7. **Emulsion polymerisation** of alkyl cyanoacrylates in an acidic aqueous medium (anionic polymerisation initiated by OH⁻); fast and done in water.
8. **Interfacial polymerisation** for nanocapsules.

**For lipid and polysaccharide systems**

9. **High-pressure homogenisation** for SLN/NLC — *hot* homogenisation (lipid melt emulsified above its melting point, then cooled) or *cold* homogenisation (solidified lipid milled and homogenised in cold surfactant solution; better for heat-labile and hydrophilic drugs).
10. **Microemulsion dilution**, **solvent emulsification–evaporation**, **double emulsion** and **membrane contactor** methods for SLN.
11. **Ionic gelation / polyelectrolyte complexation** — chitosan cross-linked with sodium tripolyphosphate, or chitosan–alginate complexes; mild and aqueous, ideal for proteins and nucleic acids.
12. **Desolvation / coacervation** for albumin and gelatin nanoparticles, followed by cross-linking (glutaraldehyde or glutamine transaminase).
13. **Self-assembly** of block copolymers (direct dissolution, dialysis, film hydration) for micelles.
14. **Media milling and high-pressure homogenisation** for nanocrystals.

### d. Evaluation of nanoparticles

| Parameter | Method | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Particle size and polydispersity index (PDI) | Dynamic light scattering / photon correlation spectroscopy; laser diffraction for larger systems | PDI below about 0.3 means a narrow distribution |
| Zeta potential | Laser Doppler electrophoresis | Beyond about ±30 mV usually means good electrostatic stability |
| Morphology | SEM, TEM, cryo-TEM, atomic force microscopy | Confirms shape, surface, nanocapsule wall |
| Drug loading and entrapment efficiency | Separate free drug by ultracentrifugation, ultrafiltration, dialysis or gel filtration, then assay | Loading % = drug in particles / total particle weight; EE % = entrapped drug / total drug added |
| Physical state of drug and lipid | DSC, powder X-ray diffraction | Shows amorphous drug, polymorphic transitions of SLN |
| Surface chemistry | FTIR, XPS, NMR | Confirms conjugation of ligand or PEG |
| In-vitro release | Dialysis bag, reverse dialysis, sample-and-separate, Franz cell; fitted to zero-order, first-order, Higuchi and Korsmeyer–Peppas models | Burst release is common |
| Residual solvent and monomer | Gas chromatography | ICH Q3C limits |
| Stability | Size, PDI, zeta, drug content and release on storage; freeze-drying with cryoprotectant | Aggregation and drug expulsion are the usual failures |
| Sterility, endotoxin, osmolarity, pH | Pharmacopoeial tests | Parenteral products |
| Biological | Cytotoxicity (MTT), haemolysis, cell uptake (flow cytometry, confocal microscopy), protein corona, pharmacokinetics and biodistribution | |

### e. Advantages, limitations and applications

**Advantages**: pass through the smallest capillaries and are taken up by cells; raise the solubility, dissolution rate and oral bioavailability of poorly soluble drugs; protect labile drugs; give sustained or triggered release; can carry a targeting ligand; usable by injection, by mouth, by the ocular, nasal and pulmonary routes.
**Limitations**: small size and large surface give aggregation and burst release; drug loading is often low; some materials are toxic or poorly cleared; dose dumping and residual solvents; costly aseptic manufacture; difficult scale-up and regulatory characterisation.
**Applications**: cancer chemotherapy; delivery to the brain; antimicrobial and antitubercular therapy; vaccines and adjuvants; gene and siRNA delivery (lipid nanoparticles); ocular and pulmonary delivery; diagnostics and theranostics.

## 2.3 Liposomes

**Liposomes** are vesicles in which one or more concentric phospholipid **bilayers** enclose aqueous compartments. They were described by Alec Bangham in the 1960s. Water-soluble drug sits in the aqueous core, lipid-soluble drug within the bilayer, and amphiphilic drug at the interface.

```text
                 Unilamellar vesicle
            o o o o o o o o o o o o
        o                             o        o   = polar head group
      o    ─────────────────────────    o      ─   = hydrocarbon chains
     o    (  aqueous core: hydrophilic   )  o
     o    (  drug                        )  o      lipophilic drug lies
      o    ─────────────────────────    o          inside the bilayer
        o                             o
            o o o o o o o o o o o o
```

### a. Components

| Component | Function | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Phospholipid | Forms the bilayer | Phosphatidylcholine (egg or soy lecithin), hydrogenated soy PC, DPPC, DSPC, DOPE, phosphatidylglycerol, sphingomyelin |
| Cholesterol (up to about 30–50 mol%) | Fills gaps between chains, raises packing order, reduces permeability and serum-induced leakage, abolishes the sharp phase transition | Cholesterol |
| Charge inducer | Prevents aggregation; cationic lipids bind nucleic acids | Stearylamine, DOTAP, DOTMA (+); dicetyl phosphate, phosphatidylserine (−) |
| Steric stabiliser | Long circulation | PEG2000-DSPE |
| Antioxidant / chelator | Protects unsaturated lipids | α-tocopherol, EDTA |

Two physical properties govern behaviour: the **phase transition temperature (Tc)** — below Tc the bilayer is a rigid gel, above it is liquid-crystalline and leaky (DPPC about 41 °C, DSPC about 55 °C, egg PC below 0 °C) — and the **packing parameter** of the lipid, which decides whether bilayers or micelles form.

### b. Classification

| Basis | Types |
| --- | --- |
| Size and lamellarity | Small unilamellar vesicles (SUV, about 20–100 nm), large unilamellar vesicles (LUV, above about 100 nm), giant unilamellar vesicles (above 1 µm), multilamellar vesicles (MLV, about 0.5–5 µm), oligolamellar and multivesicular vesicles |
| Composition / function | Conventional; long-circulating (stealth, PEGylated); immunoliposomes (antibody or Fab on the surface); cationic (gene delivery); pH-sensitive (DOPE + cholesteryl hemisuccinate or oleic acid); thermosensitive (DPPC-rich, release near 41–43 °C); magnetic; archaeosomes (archaebacterial lipids); virosomes (viral envelope proteins); transfersomes and ethosomes (ultradeformable, for skin); bubble liposomes for ultrasound |
| Preparation method | MLV by hand-shaking, REV, FATMLV, DRV, proliposomes |

### c. Methods of preparation

**1. Passive loading — mechanical dispersion**

- **Thin-film hydration (Bangham method)**: lipids and lipophilic drug are dissolved in chloroform–methanol in a round-bottom flask; the solvent is removed on a rotary evaporator under reduced pressure to leave a thin dry film; traces of solvent are removed under vacuum; the film is hydrated above Tc with the aqueous drug solution, with gentle shaking or rotation, giving heterogeneous MLVs. Annealing above Tc improves uniformity.
- **Sonication** (bath or probe) of MLVs gives SUVs; probe sonication risks metal shedding, lipid degradation and local heating.
- **Extrusion** through stacked polycarbonate membranes of defined pore size (400 → 200 → 100 nm) above Tc gives uniform LUVs with low PDI — the standard laboratory and pilot-scale sizing method.
- **French pressure cell**: MLVs forced through a narrow orifice at high pressure; gentle, good for labile material.
- **Microfluidisation** and **high-pressure homogenisation**: scalable, continuous.
- **Freeze–thaw cycling** and **dehydration–rehydration (DRV)**: raise aqueous entrapment considerably.

**2. Solvent dispersion**

- **Ethanol injection**: lipid–ethanol solution injected rapidly through a fine needle into the aqueous phase gives SUVs; simple, but dilute and ethanol must be removed.
- **Ether injection**: lipids in ether injected slowly into warm aqueous phase above the ether boiling point; ether evaporates and LUVs form; higher entrapment, slow.
- **Reverse-phase evaporation (REV)**: aqueous drug solution is emulsified (w/o) into lipid dissolved in diethyl ether or isopropyl ether; the organic solvent is removed under reduced pressure, the system passes through a viscous gel, and the gel collapses into large unilamellar vesicles. Gives high aqueous entrapment (often quoted as about 50%), so it suits expensive, water-soluble actives; drug is exposed to organic solvent and sonication.
- **Double emulsion** and **microfluidic** methods for precise control.

**3. Detergent removal**: lipids are solubilised as mixed micelles with a detergent (sodium cholate, octyl glucoside, Triton X-100); the detergent is removed by dialysis, gel filtration (Sephadex), adsorption on polystyrene beads or dilution, and bilayers close into homogeneous vesicles. Gentle; slow; residual detergent must be tested for.

**4. Active (remote) loading — the industrially important method.** A transmembrane gradient is created, and an amphipathic weak base or acid is added to preformed empty liposomes; the neutral form crosses the bilayer and is trapped inside in its ionised or precipitated form. Methods: **pH gradient** (citrate buffer pH 4 inside, pH 7.4 outside), **ammonium sulfate gradient** (used for doxorubicin, which precipitates inside as a gel-like sulfate salt), **calcium acetate gradient** for weak acids, and ionophore-based (A23187) metal-ion gradients. Entrapment efficiencies above 90% and good retention are achieved — this is how liposomal anthracyclines are made.

**5. Proliposomes**: a dry, free-flowing powder of lipid and drug coated on a soluble carrier (sorbitol, sodium chloride), which forms liposomes on adding water; solves the stability problem of aqueous dispersions.

**Processing after preparation**: separation of free drug (gel filtration, dialysis, ultracentrifugation, ion-exchange), sizing (extrusion, homogenisation), sterilisation (filtration through 0.22 µm is preferred; autoclaving and irradiation damage lipids), and freeze-drying with a cryoprotectant such as trehalose or sucrose.

### d. Evaluation of liposomes

| Parameter | Method |
| --- | --- |
| Vesicle size, distribution | DLS, laser diffraction, electron microscopy, field-flow fractionation |
| Lamellarity | ³¹P-NMR with a shift reagent, freeze-fracture electron microscopy, small-angle X-ray scattering |
| Shape and surface | TEM, cryo-TEM, SEM, AFM |
| Surface charge | Zeta potential |
| Phospholipid and cholesterol content | Stewart assay / phosphate assay (Bartlett), HPLC, enzymatic cholesterol assay |
| Entrapment efficiency and drug content | Separate free drug (minicolumn centrifugation, dialysis, ultrafiltration), lyse vesicles with Triton X-100 or methanol, assay by HPLC or UV |
| Phase transition temperature and fluidity | DSC; fluorescence anisotropy with DPH |
| In-vitro release and leakage | Dialysis in buffer and in serum; calcein or carboxyfluorescein dequenching |
| Chemical stability | Lipid hydrolysis (lyso-PC by HPLC/TLC) and oxidation (conjugated dienes, malondialdehyde, peroxide value) |
| Physical stability | Size, zeta, drug retention and appearance on storage; aggregation and fusion |
| Sterility, pyrogens, osmolarity, pH | Pharmacopoeial tests |
| In-vivo | Pharmacokinetics, biodistribution (radiolabel or fluorescent label), efficacy and toxicity |

### e. Advantages, limitations and applications

**Advantages**: materials are biocompatible, biodegradable and non-immunogenic; both hydrophilic and lipophilic drugs can be carried; drug is protected; toxicity to healthy tissue is lowered; surface can be modified for long circulation or active targeting; several products are approved, so the regulatory route is established.
**Limitations**: phospholipids hydrolyse and oxidise, giving short shelf life; drug leakage and vesicle fusion on storage; low entrapment of some water-soluble drugs by passive methods; rapid MPS clearance of conventional vesicles; high cost of pure lipids; difficult sterilisation and scale-up; batch-to-batch variability.

**Applications**: anticancer therapy (PEGylated liposomal doxorubicin for Kaposi sarcoma, ovarian and breast cancer; liposomal daunorubicin; liposomal irinotecan; liposomal cytarabine); systemic fungal infection (liposomal amphotericin B, far less nephrotoxic than the deoxycholate form); vaccines and adjuvants, including virosomes and lipid-nanoparticle mRNA vaccines; gene and siRNA delivery with cationic and ionisable lipids; topical, ocular and pulmonary delivery; and diagnostic imaging.

## Remember

- Ligand coupling: EDC/NHS to –COOH, maleimide to –SH, biotin–avidin, click chemistry, post-insertion of ligand-PEG-DSPE; couple at the distal end of PEG so the ligand is accessible.
- Nanoparticle methods: solvent evaporation, nanoprecipitation, solvent diffusion, salting-out, emulsion polymerisation, ionic gelation, hot/cold high-pressure homogenisation (SLN, NLC), supercritical fluids.
- Nanoparticle evaluation: size and PDI by DLS, charge by zeta potential, shape by TEM/AFM, entrapment after separating free drug, physical state by DSC and XRD, release in a dialysis bag with Higuchi and Korsmeyer–Peppas fitting.
- Liposome structure: phospholipid + cholesterol bilayer; SUV 20–100 nm, LUV above 100 nm, MLV 0.5–5 µm; Tc of DPPC about 41 °C.
- Liposome preparation: thin-film hydration → sonication/extrusion; ethanol and ether injection; reverse-phase evaporation (high aqueous entrapment); detergent removal; **active loading** by pH or ammonium sulfate gradient (how liposomal doxorubicin is made); proliposomes for stability.
- Liposome evaluation extras over nanoparticles: lamellarity by ³¹P-NMR, phospholipid assay (Stewart/Bartlett), lyso-PC as a marker of hydrolysis, calcein dequenching for leakage, sterilise by 0.22 µm filtration.

# Unit 3: Microcapsules and microspheres, monoclonal antibodies, niosomes, aquasomes, phytosomes and electrosomes

This unit collects the micrometre-sized carriers, the most specific homing device in medicine (the monoclonal antibody), and four "-some" systems built on surfactants, ceramic cores, phospholipid complexes and electrically treated vesicles. Questions are usually "types, preparation and evaluation" or "compare X with liposomes".

## 3.1 Microcapsules and microspheres

**Microencapsulation** is the process of enclosing solids, liquids or gases in a thin polymeric coat to give particles of roughly 1–1000 µm.

| Term | Structure |
| --- | --- |
| **Microcapsule** | Reservoir type — a distinct core surrounded by a continuous wall |
| **Microsphere** | Matrix type — drug dispersed molecularly or as crystals through the polymer |
| Nanocapsule / nanosphere | The same two structures below 1 µm |

**Reasons for microencapsulation**: sustained or controlled release; taste and odour masking (chloramphenicol palmitate, paracetamol); protection from moisture, light and oxygen (vitamin A, ferrous sulfate); separation of incompatible materials in one dosage form; converting liquids and oils into free-flowing powders; reducing gastric irritation (aspirin, potassium chloride, indomethacin); improving flow and compressibility; safe handling of irritant or hygroscopic solids; and targeting.

### a. Types of microspheres

| Type | Material and purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Bio-degradable polymeric | PLGA, PLA, polycaprolactone — depot injections |
| Natural polymeric | Albumin, gelatin, chitosan, starch, alginate |
| Synthetic non-biodegradable | Polymethyl methacrylate, ethyl cellulose (oral) |
| **Magnetic** | Magnetite (Fe3O4) in albumin, chitosan or PLGA; held at the site by an external magnet |
| **Floating (hydrodynamically balanced)** | Low density, remain buoyant in gastric fluid, prolong gastric residence |
| **Radioactive** | Yttrium-90 or other isotope in resin or glass spheres, 20–30 µm, lodged in tumour capillaries for internal radiotherapy |
| **Bioadhesive / mucoadhesive** | Chitosan, carbopol, sodium CMC — adhere to nasal, buccal, ocular or GI mucosa |
| Polymeric drug–antibody (immuno-microspheres) | Antibody on the surface for active targeting |

### b. Methods of preparation

**1. Physico-chemical methods**

- **Coacervation–phase separation**, in three steps: (i) formation of three immiscible phases — vehicle, core material and coating polymer; (ii) deposition of the coating around the core; (iii) rigidisation of the coat by heat, cross-linking or desolvation.
  - *Simple coacervation*: one polymer, desolvated by a non-solvent (sodium sulfate or alcohol added to gelatin).
  - *Complex coacervation*: two oppositely charged polymers — classically gelatin (positive below its isoelectric point, about pH 4) and acacia (negative) — which attract and separate as a coacervate; cross-linked with glutaraldehyde or formaldehyde.
  - *Organic phase separation*: ethyl cellulose in cyclohexane with temperature change, or polymer–polymer incompatibility (adding polyisobutylene).
- **Solvent evaporation / extraction from emulsion**: o/w for lipophilic drugs; w/o/w double emulsion for peptides and proteins; o/o (non-aqueous) for very water-soluble drugs.
- **Ionotropic gelation**: sodium alginate droplets dropped into calcium chloride solution form calcium alginate beads; mild, entirely aqueous, excellent for cells, proteins and probiotics.
- **Emulsion cross-linking**: aqueous gelatin, albumin or chitosan emulsified in oil, then hardened by heat (thermal denaturation) or a chemical cross-linker.
- **Polymerisation** (suspension, emulsion, interfacial) and **solvent-change / salting-out** methods.

**2. Mechanical / physical methods**

- **Spray drying**: drug and polymer solution or dispersion is atomised into hot air; the solvent flashes off and microspheres are collected in a cyclone. One step, continuous, scalable; the usual industrial choice. Yield losses and heat exposure are the drawbacks.
- **Spray congealing**: molten wax or lipid carrying the drug is atomised into cold air and solidifies.
- **Air-suspension (Wurster) coating**: particles are fluidised and coating solution is sprayed from the bottom; gives very uniform films on particles above about 50 µm.
- **Pan coating** for larger particles; **multi-orifice centrifugal** (extrusion through a rotating disc); **electrostatic** methods.
- **Supercritical fluid** and **membrane emulsification** methods for narrow size distribution.

### c. Release mechanisms

Diffusion through the polymer wall or matrix (Higuchi kinetics for a matrix); erosion or degradation of the polymer (PLGA by bulk hydrolysis, typically biphasic with a burst, a lag and then an erosion-controlled phase); osmotic pressure causing cracks in the wall; and swelling-controlled release from hydrogel spheres. Release data are fitted to zero-order, first-order, Higuchi (Q = k√t) and Korsmeyer–Peppas (Mt/M∞ = kt^n) models; for spheres n ≤ 0.43 indicates Fickian diffusion and n = 0.85 case-II (erosion) transport.

### d. Evaluation of microspheres

| Parameter | Method |
| --- | --- |
| Particle size and distribution | Optical microscopy, sieve analysis, laser diffraction, Coulter counter |
| Shape and surface | SEM (surface, pores, wall thickness), TEM |
| Flow properties | Angle of repose, bulk and tapped density, Carr's index, Hausner ratio |
| Drug content, loading and entrapment efficiency | Dissolve or digest the spheres, assay by UV or HPLC |
| Drug–polymer interaction and physical state | FTIR, DSC, powder X-ray diffraction |
| Swelling index and density | Weight gain in buffer; density by pycnometry (floating systems need density below 1) |
| In-vitro release | USP dissolution apparatus, dialysis bag, flow-through cell; model fitting |
| Buoyancy (floating) | Floating lag time and total floating time in 0.1 N HCl |
| Mucoadhesion | In-vitro wash-off test on intestinal mucosa; tensile strength |
| Magnetic systems | Magnetite content, magnetic responsiveness in a field |
| Residual solvent, cross-linker and sterility | GC; tests for free glutaraldehyde; pharmacopoeial sterility |
| Stability | Size, drug content and release after storage at controlled conditions |

**Applications**: long-acting intramuscular and subcutaneous depots of peptides (PLGA microspheres for luteinising-hormone-releasing-hormone analogues and octreotide, releasing over weeks to months), vaccine single-shot delivery, chemoembolisation and radioembolisation of liver tumours, oral sustained release, nasal and pulmonary delivery, and cell encapsulation.

## 3.2 Monoclonal antibodies

**Antibodies (immunoglobulins)** are Y-shaped glycoproteins of two heavy and two light chains, with two antigen-binding fragments (Fab) carrying the hypervariable complementarity-determining regions, and a constant Fc region responsible for effector functions and for the long half-life through FcRn recycling. **Monoclonal antibodies (mAbs)** come from a single B-cell clone and recognise one epitope; **polyclonal** antisera contain many clones against many epitopes.

### a. Preparation — hybridoma technology (Köhler and Milstein, 1975)

```text
  Mouse immunised with antigen (several boosters)
        ↓
  Spleen removed → B lymphocytes (make antibody, die in culture)
        +
  Myeloma cells (immortal, HGPRT-deficient, make no antibody)
        ↓  fusion with polyethylene glycol (or electrofusion)
  Mixture of cells
        ↓  grown in HAT medium
  Hypoxanthine–aminopterin–thymidine selection:
    aminopterin blocks the de-novo nucleotide pathway;
    unfused myeloma cells lack HGPRT and cannot use the salvage pathway → die
    unfused B cells die naturally in a few days
    only HYBRIDOMAS (immortality from myeloma + HGPRT from B cell) survive
        ↓
  Screening of supernatants (ELISA, RIA) for the wanted specificity
        ↓
  Cloning by limiting dilution (one cell per well) → monoclonality
        ↓
  Expansion in culture flasks, roller bottles or bioreactors
        ↓
  Purification: ammonium sulfate precipitation → Protein A/G affinity
  chromatography → ion-exchange and size-exclusion polishing →
  viral clearance and sterile filtration
```

Modern alternatives: **recombinant and phage-display libraries** (fully human antibodies selected in vitro), **transgenic mice carrying human immunoglobulin genes**, **single-B-cell cloning**, and expression in CHO or NS0 cell lines.

### b. Types by origin

| Type | Composition | Suffix | Immunogenicity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Murine | 100% mouse | -omab | High (human anti-mouse antibody response) |
| Chimeric | Mouse variable + human constant (about 65% human) | -ximab | Moderate |
| Humanised | Only the CDRs are mouse (about 95% human) | -zumab | Low |
| Fully human | Entirely human sequence | -umab | Lowest |

**Fragments and engineered formats**: Fab, F(ab′)2, single-chain variable fragment (scFv), diabodies, nanobodies (single-domain), and bispecific antibodies that bind a tumour antigen with one arm and a T cell (CD3) with the other.

### c. Applications in targeting and therapy

1. **Naked therapeutic antibodies** — block a receptor or ligand, or recruit antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity and complement: trastuzumab (HER2), rituximab (CD20), cetuximab (EGFR), bevacizumab (VEGF), and anti-TNF-α agents in autoimmune disease.
2. **Antibody–drug conjugates (ADCs)** — a highly potent cytotoxic payload joined by a linker, released only after internalisation: trastuzumab emtansine, brentuximab vedotin, gemtuzumab ozogamicin. Design variables are the linker (cleavable hydrazone, disulfide or peptide; non-cleavable thioether), the conjugation site, and the drug-to-antibody ratio (usually about 2–4), which controls both potency and aggregation.
3. **Immunoliposomes and antibody-coated nanoparticles** — the antibody guides the whole carrier.
4. **Radioimmunoconjugates** for imaging and radioimmunotherapy.
5. **Immunotoxins** — antibody linked to a protein toxin.
6. **ADEPT** — antibody-directed enzyme prodrug therapy: the antibody–enzyme conjugate localises first, the prodrug is given later and is converted to the active drug only at the tumour.
7. **Diagnostics** — ELISA, RIA, immunohistochemistry, lateral-flow pregnancy tests, blood grouping, imaging.

**Advantages**: unmatched specificity, long half-life, many possible payloads, and defined mechanisms.
**Limitations**: large size (about 150 kDa) limits penetration into solid tumours and prevents oral use; immunogenicity; antigen heterogeneity and antigen loss cause resistance; cold-chain storage; very high cost; aggregation and other stability problems of protein formulations.

## 3.3 Niosomes

**Niosomes** are bilayer vesicles formed by hydrating **non-ionic surfactants**, usually with cholesterol and a charge inducer. Structurally they resemble liposomes but are chemically more stable and cheaper.

**Components**: sorbitan esters (Span 20, 40, 60, 80), polysorbates (Tween 20, 60, 80), polyoxyethylene alkyl ethers (Brij), alkyl glycerol ethers; **cholesterol** to give rigidity and stop leakage; **dicetyl phosphate or stearylamine** to prevent aggregation.
Surfactants with HLB roughly 4–8 form vesicles best; those of high HLB need more cholesterol. The **critical packing parameter** (CPP = v/a·lc) predicts the shape: CPP between 0.5 and 1 favours bilayer vesicles.

**Preparation**: thin-film hydration; ether injection; **reverse-phase evaporation**; **sonication**; **micro-fluidisation**; the **"bubble" method** (surfactant–cholesterol dispersion bubbled with nitrogen at about 70 °C); **transmembrane pH-gradient (remote) loading**; and the **proniosome** approach — surfactant coated on a water-soluble carrier (sorbitol, maltodextrin) as a dry, free-flowing powder that forms niosomes on adding warm water, which removes the stability problems of an aqueous dispersion.

**Evaluation**: the same list as liposomes — size and PDI, zeta potential, morphology by TEM, entrapment after separating free drug, bilayer rigidity by fluorescence probes, in-vitro release, osmotic shock and storage stability.

| Feature | Liposomes | Niosomes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bilayer former | Phospholipids | Non-ionic surfactants |
| Chemical stability | Lower (oxidation, hydrolysis to lyso-PC) | Higher — no ester-linked unsaturated fatty acids to oxidise |
| Raw material purity and cost | Natural phospholipids vary; expensive | Synthetic, uniform, cheap |
| Storage | Often under nitrogen, refrigerated | Easier; proniosomes are dry |
| Status | Several approved products | Mainly cosmetics, topical and research |

**Applications**: topical and transdermal delivery, cosmetics, anticancer and antitubercular delivery under investigation, leishmaniasis (macrophage uptake), ocular delivery, oral peptide delivery and vaccine adjuvants.

## 3.4 Aquasomes

**Aquasomes** are three-layered, self-assembled, water-like particles of roughly 60–300 nm, described as "bodies of water" because a surface water layer preserves the conformation of the adsorbed biomolecule.

```text
   [ 1 ] Ceramic / polymer CORE        — nanocrystalline calcium phosphate
            (hydroxyapatite), ceramic diamond, tin oxide, brushite
                    ↓ coated with
   [ 2 ] Polyhydroxy oligomeric FILM   — cellobiose, trehalose, sucrose,
            pyridoxal-5-phosphate, citrate
                    ↓ adsorption
   [ 3 ] Therapeutic agent (DRUG)      — protein, peptide, enzyme, antigen,
            insulin, haemoglobin
```

**Principle**: the sugar coat replaces the hydration shell of the protein, so the protein keeps its native three-dimensional structure and activity — "molecular shielding". Binding of the drug is non-covalent (ionic, hydrogen bonding, van der Waals), so the drug is released in its active form.

**Preparation (three stages)**

1. **Core formation** — nanocrystalline hydroxyapatite by co-precipitation from calcium chloride and disodium hydrogen phosphate solutions with pH control, or by inverted-micelle, sonication or plasma condensation methods; the core is sonicated, filtered and freeze-dried.
2. **Coating** — the core is dispersed in a solution of the polyhydroxy oligomer, stirred and sonicated so that the sugar adsorbs; unadsorbed sugar is removed by centrifugation and the product is lyophilised.
3. **Drug loading** — the coated cores are incubated in a cold buffered solution of the drug at a suitable pH; the drug adsorbs on the sugar layer and the product is freeze-dried.

**Evaluation**: core size and crystallinity (XRD, SEM, TEM), sugar coating (FTIR, carbohydrate assay such as the phenol–sulfuric acid or anthrone method), drug loading, in-vitro release, retention of biological activity (for example enzyme assay or immunogenicity of an adsorbed antigen), haemocompatibility and stability.

**Advantages**: protects fragile proteins from denaturation; no chemical modification of the drug; good physical stability as a dry powder; large surface for loading; biodegradable and biocompatible core.
**Limitations**: only drugs that adsorb well can be carried; loading is limited; burst release is possible; scale-up and reproducible core preparation are difficult.
**Applications**: delivery of insulin, haemoglobin (as an oxygen carrier), enzymes such as serratiopeptidase, antigens and vaccine adjuvants, and some antibiotics and anti-inflammatory drugs.

## 3.5 Phytosomes

**Phytosomes** (phospholipid complexes of phytoconstituents) are formed when a standardised plant extract or a polar phytoconstituent — usually a flavonoid or a terpenoid — reacts with phosphatidylcholine, commonly in a 1:1 or 1:2 molar ratio. The polar head of the phospholipid binds the phytoconstituent by hydrogen bonding, while the fatty-acid chains face outward, forming a lipophilic envelope.

**Why they are needed**: many useful phytoconstituents (silymarin, curcumin, quercetin, rutin, green-tea catechins, ginkgo flavonoids, glycyrrhizin, boswellic acids) are large, polar or poorly water-soluble molecules, so they are poorly absorbed from the gut. The complex is lipid-soluble enough to cross the enterocyte membrane, which raises bioavailability several-fold.

**Difference from liposomes**: in a liposome the drug is *dissolved in the aqueous core or dispersed in the bilayer*, with hundreds or thousands of phospholipid molecules per vesicle and no chemical bond; in a phytosome the phytoconstituent is **chemically bonded (by hydrogen bonds) to the polar head of the phospholipid**, giving a defined molecular complex — confirmed by shifts in ¹H- and ¹³C-NMR signals of the phospholipid head group.

**Preparation**: the phytoconstituent and phosphatidylcholine are refluxed in an aprotic solvent (dichloromethane, ethyl acetate, dioxane) at a controlled temperature; the solvent is reduced and the complex precipitated with a non-solvent (n-hexane) and filtered, or the solvent is removed by evaporation, lyophilisation or spray drying.

**Evaluation**: confirmation of complex formation by DSC (disappearance or shift of melting endotherms), FTIR, ¹H/¹³C-NMR and powder X-ray diffraction; solubility in water and n-octanol; particle size and zeta potential of the dispersion; entrapment/complexation efficiency; in-vitro dissolution and ex-vivo permeation; and in-vivo bioavailability and pharmacodynamic studies (for example liver-protective activity for silymarin phytosome).

**Advantages**: markedly better absorption and bioavailability, lower effective dose, protection of the constituent from gut and bacterial degradation, improved skin penetration in cosmetics, and good stability.
**Limitations**: the phytoconstituent must have a suitable group to hydrogen-bond with the phospholipid; limited loading; rapid clearance of the free complex; and standardisation of the extract is essential.

## 3.6 Electrosomes

**Electrosomes** are vesicular carriers prepared or loaded with the help of an **electrical field**. Two senses are used in the literature, and both are acceptable in an answer:

1. **Electroformation of vesicles.** Lipid is deposited as a thin film on conducting electrodes (indium tin oxide glass or platinum wires), the chamber is filled with the aqueous phase, and a low-voltage alternating field (typically a few volts at about 10 Hz) is applied. The field causes the hydrated lipid film to swell and bud off, producing large, mostly unilamellar vesicles of very uniform size. The method is gentle, solvent-free and used especially to make giant unilamellar vesicles for research and for encapsulating cells and macromolecules.
2. **Electroporation-assisted loading.** Preformed vesicles (or cells, as in resealed erythrocytes) are exposed to short high-voltage pulses that create transient aqueous pores in the bilayer; drug, protein or nucleic acid in the surrounding medium diffuses in, and the pores reseal when the field is removed. This gives high loading of large, hydrophilic molecules that cannot be loaded passively or by a pH gradient.

**Evaluation** follows the liposome list — size and lamellarity, zeta potential, entrapment efficiency, retention of activity of the loaded macromolecule, membrane integrity after resealing, and release.

**Advantages**: uniform, largely unilamellar vesicles; no organic solvent or detergent; loading of fragile macromolecules under mild conditions.
**Limitations**: low yield and dilute product; specialised apparatus; ionic strength of the medium is restricted in electroformation; pulse conditions must be optimised or the vesicles lyse.

## Remember

- Microcapsule = reservoir (core + wall); microsphere = matrix. Microencapsulation is used for sustained release, taste masking, protection, separating incompatibles and converting liquids to powders.
- Coacervation has three steps: three-phase formation → deposition of coat → rigidisation. Complex coacervation uses gelatin + acacia; simple coacervation uses a desolvating agent.
- Spray drying is the usual industrial method; ionotropic gelation (alginate + calcium chloride) is the mild aqueous method; PLGA solvent evaporation gives peptide depots.
- Hybridoma: spleen B cell + HGPRT-deficient myeloma, fused with PEG, selected in HAT medium, screened by ELISA, cloned by limiting dilution. Suffixes: -omab murine, -ximab chimeric, -zumab humanised, -umab human.
- ADC design: potent payload, cleavable or non-cleavable linker, drug-to-antibody ratio about 2–4.
- Niosomes: non-ionic surfactant (Span, Tween, Brij) + cholesterol + charge inducer; more chemically stable and cheaper than liposomes; proniosomes are the dry form.
- Aquasomes are three-layered: ceramic core (hydroxyapatite) → polyhydroxy oligomer (cellobiose, trehalose) → adsorbed protein; the sugar layer protects protein conformation.
- Phytosome = phytoconstituent **hydrogen-bonded** to the polar head of phosphatidylcholine (a molecular complex, not a vesicle) — used to raise the bioavailability of flavonoids such as silymarin and curcumin.
- Electrosomes: vesicles formed by an alternating electric field on a lipid-coated electrode, or loaded by electroporation pulses — gentle, solvent-free, good for macromolecules.

# Unit 4: Pulmonary and intranasal drug delivery systems

The lung and the nose are the two mucosal routes that combine a very large or very permeable surface with easy, non-invasive access. The syllabus asks for aerosols, propellants, containers, types, preparation and evaluation for the pulmonary route, and the same four headings for the intranasal route.

## 4.1 Why the lung

| Feature | Value / note |
| --- | --- |
| Alveolar surface area | Roughly 70–100 m² in an adult |
| Alveolar epithelium | Type I pneumocytes, about 0.1–0.5 µm thick |
| Blood supply | The entire cardiac output passes through the pulmonary circulation |
| Metabolism | Low first-pass metabolism; fewer drug-metabolising enzymes than the liver or gut |
| Onset | Very rapid for both local and systemic action |

**Advantages**: small dose for a local effect in asthma and COPD, so fewer systemic side effects; rapid onset; avoidance of hepatic first pass and of the harsh gastric environment; useful for peptides and proteins; needle-free.
**Limitations**: efficiency depends heavily on the patient's inspiratory effort and technique; much of the dose is lost in the device, mouth and throat; mucociliary clearance and alveolar macrophages remove the drug; local irritation and cough; the lung's defence mechanisms limit the dose; dose reproducibility is harder than for an oral tablet.

### Mechanisms of deposition and the aerodynamic diameter

Deposition is governed by the **mass median aerodynamic diameter (MMAD)**, defined as the diameter of a unit-density sphere with the same settling velocity as the particle: d_ae = d_geo × √(ρ/χ), where ρ is particle density and χ the dynamic shape factor. A porous, low-density particle can therefore be large geometrically (which stops aggregation and macrophage uptake) while still being small aerodynamically.

| Mechanism | Dominant particle size | Region |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inertial impaction | Above about 5 µm | Oropharynx and large conducting airways (fast, turbulent flow) |
| Sedimentation (gravity) | About 1–5 µm | Smaller bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli — helped by breath-holding |
| Brownian diffusion | Below about 0.5 µm | Alveoli, but much is exhaled again |

**The respirable fraction is therefore about 1–5 µm**; above this the drug lands in the throat and is swallowed, below about 0.5 µm it is largely breathed out. Other factors: inspiratory flow rate (slow and deep for a pressurised inhaler, fast and forceful for a dry powder inhaler), breath-holding for about 10 seconds, airway geometry and disease, hygroscopic growth of the droplet, and particle charge.

**Clearance**: the mucociliary escalator removes material deposited on ciliated airways within hours; alveolar macrophages phagocytose particles of about 1–3 µm in the alveoli; absorption into the blood, and metabolism, remove the rest.

## 4.2 Pharmaceutical aerosols

A **pharmaceutical aerosol** is a pressurised dosage form in which the therapeutically active ingredient is dissolved, suspended or emulsified in a propellant or a mixture of propellant and solvent, and is expelled as a fine dispersion of liquid or solid particles when the valve is opened.

### a. Components

```text
   ┌─────────────┐  actuator (mouthpiece, spray orifice)
   │   ╔═══╗     │
   │   ║   ║     │  metering valve + stem, gasket, spring
   │ ──╨───╨──   │  valve ferrule crimped to the can
   │   ░░░░░░    │  vapour phase of propellant
   │   ▓▓▓▓▓▓    │  liquid: drug + propellant (+ cosolvent, surfactant)
   │   │dip│     │  dip tube reaching the bottom
   └───┴───┴─────┘  container: aluminium / stainless steel / coated glass
```

| Part | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| **Propellant** | Provides the energy; may also be the solvent or vehicle |
| **Container** | Must withstand pressures up to about 140–180 psig; aluminium (seamless, often internally lacquered with epoxy or fluoropolymer to stop drug adsorption and corrosion), stainless steel, or plastic-coated glass for low-pressure products |
| **Valve** | *Continuous* valve for topical products; **metering valve** for inhalers, delivering a reproducible 25–100 µL per actuation. Parts: ferrule, mounting cup, stem, gasket (nitrile, neoprene — a source of extractables), spring, dip tube, metering chamber |
| **Actuator** | Decides the spray pattern and droplet size through the orifice diameter and expansion chamber; types are spray, foam, solid-stream, and the special oral and nasal adaptors |
| **Product concentrate** | Drug, cosolvent (ethanol), surfactant/suspending agent (oleic acid, lecithin, sorbitan trioleate), antioxidant, flavour |

### b. Propellants

A propellant is a liquefied gas or compressed gas that supplies the pressure to expel the contents and to atomise them.

| Class | Examples | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs)** | Propellant 11 (trichlorofluoromethane), 12 (dichlorodifluoromethane), 114 (dichlorotetrafluoroethane) | Historic standard; blended to adjust vapour pressure; **phased out under the Montreal Protocol** because they deplete stratospheric ozone |
| **Hydrofluoroalkanes (HFA)** | HFA-134a (tetrafluoroethane), HFA-227ea (heptafluoropropane) | Present-day inhaler propellants; no chlorine, so no ozone depletion. They are poor solvents for the old surfactants, so formulations had to be redeveloped with ethanol as cosolvent and new valve elastomers; they do have a high global-warming potential, which is driving a further change to low-GWP propellants |
| **Hydrocarbons** | Propane, n-butane, isobutane | Cheap, low toxicity, no ozone effect, but **flammable**; used in topical and non-inhalation products |
| **Compressed gases** | Nitrogen, carbon dioxide, nitrous oxide | Inert; pressure falls as the product is used; give a wet spray or foam rather than a fine mist |
| **Dimethyl ether** | | Good solvent, but flammable |

Vapour pressure is adjusted by **blending** propellants and is predicted by Raoult's law (P = P_A x_A + P_B x_B).

### c. Types of aerosol systems

| System | Description |
| --- | --- |
| **Two-phase (solution)** | Liquid (drug dissolved in propellant ± cosolvent) + vapour. Simplest; fine mist; needs the drug to be soluble |
| **Three-phase (suspension)** | Drug micronised and suspended in propellant, with a surfactant to prevent caking; must be shaken before use. Most older inhalers are of this type |
| **Three-phase (emulsion)** | Aqueous phase + propellant + vapour; gives a **foam** (stable, quick-breaking or thermal) when the propellant is in the internal phase |
| **Barrier (separate-compartment) systems** | A piston or collapsible bag separates product from propellant (compressed gas); the product leaves without propellant contact — used for sterile and viscous products |

### d. Devices for pulmonary delivery

**1. Pressurised metered-dose inhaler (pMDI)**
Drug in solution or suspension in HFA propellant with a metering valve. Each actuation gives a fixed dose. Cheap, portable, sealed and dose-reproducible, but requires the patient to coordinate actuation with a slow deep breath, and much of the dose impacts in the oropharynx because the plume leaves at high speed. **Spacers / valved holding chambers** solve both problems by slowing the plume and allowing the large particles to settle out. Breath-actuated pMDIs remove the need for coordination. Formulation issues: suspension flocculation and caking, valve clogging, moisture ingress, loss of prime, and "tail-off" of dose at the end of the canister — hence dose counters.

**2. Dry powder inhaler (DPI)**
Micronised drug (1–5 µm) is usually blended with a coarse carrier, most often **α-lactose monohydrate (about 50–100 µm)**, to improve flow and dose uniformity; the fine drug must detach from the carrier during inhalation. Energy comes from the patient's own inspiratory flow, so no coordination is needed and no propellant is used, but performance depends on inspiratory effort and the device's internal resistance, and powders are sensitive to humidity. Types: single-dose capsule-based, multi-dose reservoir, and multi-unit blister devices. Advances include engineered particles (spray-dried, large porous, co-spray-dried with leucine) and force-control agents such as magnesium stearate.

**3. Nebulisers**
Convert a solution or suspension into a mist breathed over several minutes during tidal breathing — useful for infants, the elderly, the very breathless and for large doses.
- *Jet (air-jet) nebulisers*: compressed gas through a Venturi draws liquid up and shatters it; baffles return large droplets. Cheap, but slow and some drug is wasted during exhalation (solved by breath-enhanced and breath-actuated designs).
- *Ultrasonic nebulisers*: a piezoelectric crystal vibrating at 1–3 MHz raises a fountain of droplets. Fast, quiet, but heats the fluid (bad for proteins) and handles suspensions poorly.
- *Vibrating-mesh nebulisers*: fluid is pushed through thousands of laser-drilled holes; efficient, low residual volume, gentle on proteins, portable.

**4. Soft-mist inhaler**: mechanical energy (a spring) forces solution through a fine nozzle system to give a slow-moving, long-lasting mist with a high fine-particle fraction, with no propellant.

**Dosage forms for the lung**: solutions, suspensions, dry powders, liposomal dispersions (liposomal amikacin and amphotericin for lung infections), nanoparticles and microparticles for sustained lung release, and vaccines.

### e. Preparation of aerosols

1. **Manufacture of the concentrate** — micronisation of the drug (jet milling or spray drying) to 1–5 µm; mixing with cosolvent, surfactant and other excipients in a closed, moisture-controlled area; or preparation of the solution.
2. **Filling**
   - **Cold filling**: the concentrate and the chilled propellant (about −40 °C) are metered into the chilled can and the valve is crimped on at once. Simple, but unsuitable for aqueous and heat-labile products and there is a moisture-condensation risk.
   - **Pressure filling**: the concentrate is added at room temperature, the valve is crimped, air is evacuated, and propellant is forced in through the valve under pressure. Preferred: less propellant loss, less moisture, suitable for most products — the method used for inhalers.
   - **Compressed-gas filling** for products using nitrogen or carbon dioxide.
3. **Crimping of the valve** to a controlled depth and collet diameter.
4. **Leak testing** in a water bath at about 50–55 °C, weight-loss testing over time, and spray testing of samples.
5. **Capping, labelling and packing**; the label must carry the flammability and pressure warnings.

### f. Evaluation of pulmonary products

| Test | Purpose and method |
| --- | --- |
| **Aerodynamic particle size distribution** | The key test: **cascade impactor** (Andersen eight-stage, or the Next Generation Impactor) or multistage liquid impinger. Each stage collects a size band; the drug on each stage is assayed; MMAD, geometric standard deviation and the **fine particle fraction / fine particle dose** (usually the mass below 5 µm) are calculated |
| **Delivered (emitted) dose and dose uniformity** | Dose unit sampling apparatus; tested at the beginning, middle and end of the canister or device |
| Vapour pressure and leakage | Pressure gauge, water-bath leak test, weight loss |
| Spray pattern and plume geometry | Impaction on a treated plate or laser imaging |
| Net content, moisture, foreign particulates | Weight of filled and emptied container; Karl Fischer |
| Valve delivery (shot weight) | Mass of two actuations after priming |
| Flammability and combustibility | Flame extension and closed-drum tests for hydrocarbon propellants |
| Dissolution / in-vitro release and permeation | For sustained-release inhaled particles |
| Microbiological quality, preservative efficacy | For aqueous nebuliser solutions |
| Biological tests | Deposition imaging (gamma scintigraphy), pharmacokinetics, local tolerability |

## 4.3 Intranasal drug delivery

### a. The nasal route

The nasal cavity has a total surface of about **150 cm²** and three regions:

| Region | Features | Role in delivery |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nasal vestibule | Anterior, squamous epithelium, hairs | Filters particles; poor absorption |
| Respiratory region (turbinates) | Largest area; pseudostratified columnar ciliated epithelium with microvilli; very rich blood supply | **Main site of systemic absorption** |
| Olfactory region | About 3–10 cm² at the roof; olfactory neurons pass through the cribriform plate | **Nose-to-brain transport** |

**Advantages**: rapid absorption and onset, comparable with intravenous for some small lipophilic drugs; avoids hepatic first-pass metabolism and gastrointestinal degradation; large, highly vascular surface; easy, needle-free self-administration, so good patient acceptance; possible direct nose-to-brain delivery; useful for vaccines (mucosal IgA response).
**Limitations**: volume limited to about 25–200 µL per nostril; **mucociliary clearance** removes the formulation in about 15–20 min; enzymes in the mucosa (peptidases, proteases, cytochrome P450) degrade peptides; large hydrophilic molecules absorb poorly; absorption changes in the common cold, rhinitis and allergy; possible irritation, ciliotoxicity and long-term mucosal damage; the dose that can be given is small.

**Mechanisms of absorption**: transcellular passive diffusion of lipophilic drugs; the aqueous paracellular route through tight junctions for small hydrophilic molecules; carrier-mediated transport; and transcytosis for larger molecules. Nose-to-brain transport proceeds by the **olfactory pathway** (intraneuronal axonal transport, slow; and extraneuronal perineural transport along the olfactory nerve into the cerebrospinal fluid, fast) and the **trigeminal pathway**.

**Factors affecting nasal absorption**: molecular weight (absorption falls sharply above about 1 kDa without an enhancer), lipophilicity and degree of ionisation (the nasal surface pH is about 5.5–6.5), solubility and dissolution rate of the particles, pH, osmolarity and viscosity of the formulation, volume and concentration, deposition site (anterior deposition is cleared more slowly than posterior), and the device's spray angle and droplet size (droplets of about 10–50 µm stay in the nose; below 10 µm they may reach the lung).

### b. Types of nasal dosage forms

| Form | Comment |
| --- | --- |
| **Solutions and suspensions (drops)** | Simple and cheap, but the dose is not reproducible and the drops drain quickly to the throat |
| **Metered sprays (mechanical pump)** | The standard form: reproducible dose, better deposition in the turbinates, less drainage |
| **Aerosols (pMDI with a nasal adaptor)** | Reproducible dose, protection from contamination; propellant may irritate |
| **Gels and in-situ gelling systems** | Thermosensitive (poloxamer 407), pH-sensitive (carbopol), ion-sensitive (gellan gum, deacetylated gellan) — liquid in the bottle, gel in the nose, so residence time rises |
| **Powders** | Better stability, no preservative, longer residence; may irritate |
| **Microspheres and nanoparticles** | Chitosan, starch, alginate: mucoadhesive, protect peptides, prolong contact, open tight junctions |
| **Liposomes, niosomes, nanoemulsions, microemulsions** | Protect the drug and improve permeation; used in nose-to-brain research |
| **Inserts and bioadhesive films** | Prolonged local contact |

**Excipients**: buffers (pH about 4.5–6.5), tonicity adjusters (sodium chloride, dextrose; isotonic or slightly hypertonic is preferred), **permeation enhancers** (chitosan, bile salts, fatty acids, cyclodextrins, phospholipids, surfactants — ciliotoxicity must be checked), **mucoadhesives** (chitosan, carbopol, hydroxypropyl methylcellulose, sodium hyaluronate), viscosity modifiers, enzyme inhibitors (bestatin, aprotinin), preservatives (benzalkonium chloride, phenylethyl alcohol — ciliotoxicity is a concern, hence preservative-free multidose devices) and antioxidants.

### c. Preparation

Nasal solutions and suspensions are prepared like other sterile or low-bioburden aqueous products: the drug and excipients are dissolved in water for injection, the pH, tonicity and viscosity are adjusted, the solution is filtered (0.22 µm) and filled into the spray container under controlled conditions; suspensions need micronised drug and a wetting agent. Gels are prepared by hydrating the polymer at low temperature. Microspheres and nanoparticles are prepared by the methods of Units 2 and 3 (spray drying, ionic gelation, emulsion solvent evaporation) and then dispersed in the vehicle or filled as a powder. Containers: amber glass or plastic bottles with a metering spray pump and actuator, unit-dose or bi-dose devices for emergency and nose-to-brain products, and preservative-free multidose systems with a filter or a one-way valve.

### d. Evaluation of nasal products

| Test | Method / purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Appearance, pH, osmolality, viscosity, surface tension | Routine physical quality |
| Drug content, content uniformity, impurities | HPLC |
| **Spray pattern and plume geometry** | Impaction and imaging at set distances; shows how the dose spreads in the cavity |
| **Droplet size distribution** | Laser diffraction; droplets of about 10–50 µm stay in the nose; the fraction below 10 µm must be low to avoid lung deposition |
| Shot weight and dose per actuation; uniformity through the container | Gravimetric and assay, at beginning, middle and end |
| Gelation temperature / gelling capacity | For in-situ gels |
| **Mucoadhesive strength and nasal residence** | Texture analyser, wash-off test; gamma scintigraphy or fluorescence in vivo |
| **Ex-vivo permeation** | Sheep, goat or bovine nasal mucosa in a Franz diffusion cell; flux and permeability coefficient |
| **Ciliotoxicity / ciliary beat frequency** | Frog palate or excised mucosa; essential when an enhancer is used |
| **Histopathology of the mucosa** | After repeated dosing |
| Microbial limits, sterility (if claimed), preservative efficacy | Pharmacopoeial |
| In-vivo | Pharmacokinetics; for brain targeting the drug targeting efficiency and direct transport percentage are calculated from the brain and plasma AUC after nasal and intravenous dosing |

**Marketed and studied uses**: decongestants and topical corticosteroids for rhinitis; antihistamines; sumatriptan and other migraine treatments; desmopressin and calcitonin (peptides); hormone and vitamin B12 products; emergency products for opioid overdose and for seizure clusters; live attenuated influenza vaccine; and intranasal insulin and neuropeptides as nose-to-brain research areas.

## Remember

- Respirable (fine particle) size is **1–5 µm**; above 5 µm impaction in the throat, below 0.5 µm is exhaled. MMAD = d_geo√(ρ/χ), which is why large porous particles work.
- Aerosol components: propellant, container, valve (metering valve for inhalers, 25–100 µL), actuator, product concentrate. Systems: two-phase solution, three-phase suspension or emulsion (foam), barrier.
- Propellants: CFCs (11, 12, 114) withdrawn under the Montreal Protocol → **HFA-134a and HFA-227ea** for inhalers; hydrocarbons and compressed gases for topical products.
- Devices: pMDI (needs coordination; use a spacer), DPI (lactose carrier, patient's own inspiratory effort), nebulisers (jet, ultrasonic, vibrating mesh), soft-mist inhaler.
- Filling: cold filling or, preferably, **pressure filling**; then crimping, leak testing in a 50–55 °C water bath, and spray testing.
- Key inhaler test = **cascade impactor** (Andersen or NGI) giving MMAD, GSD and fine particle fraction; plus delivered dose uniformity.
- Nasal cavity about 150 cm²: vestibule (filter), respiratory region (systemic absorption), olfactory region 3–10 cm² (nose-to-brain). Volume about 25–200 µL, mucociliary clearance about 15–20 min, surface pH about 5.5–6.5.
- Nasal strategies: mucoadhesives (chitosan, carbopol), in-situ gels (poloxamer 407, gellan gum), permeation enhancers, enzyme inhibitors, micro- and nanoparticles.
- Nasal evaluation extras: spray pattern, droplet size (keep the fraction below 10 µm low), gelation temperature, ex-vivo permeation through excised mucosa, and ciliotoxicity.
